articles.title: A century before it happened elsewhere: how the first printing press reached the continent
articles.excerpt: Historians detail how bilingual books were being printed decades earlier than commonly assumed.
articles.author: victor-lenore
articles.imageCaption: A woodcut depicting an early printing workshop | EP
content: Historians have detailed how the first printing press on the continent began producing bilingual books decades earlier than commonly assumed.
The findings, based on newly catalogued archival material, suggest a far more active early printing culture than previously documented.
Researchers say the discovery could reshape how the period's literacy and publishing history is taught.

articles.title: Profile: the intellectual whose theories on independence keep resurfacing in debate
articles.excerpt: A closer look at the writer whose arguments continue to divide opinion decades after they were first published.
articles.author: victor-lenore
articles.imageCaption: A portrait of the writer in his study | EP
content: The writer's arguments continue to resurface in political debate decades after they were first published, despite being widely disputed at the time.
Supporters describe the work as prescient; critics call it a dangerous simplification of a far more complicated history.
Either way, the renewed attention says as much about the present moment as it does about the original text.

articles.title: Review: a tightly wound thriller that resists easy answers
articles.excerpt: The film's refusal to moralize is either its greatest strength or its biggest risk, depending on who you ask.
articles.author: victor-lenore
articles.imageCaption: A still from the film's closing scene | Distributor
content: The film's refusal to moralize is either its greatest strength or its biggest risk, depending on who you ask.
What is not in question is the craft on display, from the editing to a lead performance that carries long stretches of near-silence.
It will not be for everyone, but it lingers well past the credits.

articles.title: Ernest Hemingway reflects on Spain: "If the Spanish people have any common trait, it is pride, and if they have another, it is common sense."
articles.excerpt: A look back at the writer's decades-long relationship with the country and the people who shaped his work.
articles.author: victor-lenore
articles.imageCaption: Ernest Hemingway at his writing desk | Archive
content: The writer's long relationship with the country left a visible mark on much of his major work, from bullfighting to the civil war years.
Biographers point to a handful of friendships formed during his travels there as especially formative, shaping both his fiction and his public persona.
Decades later, his observations about the country's character are still quoted regularly in cultural commentary.
